name: Fraxel (Fraxel Restore / Dual)

lead: Fraxel is a brand of fractional lasers used to improve scars, sun damage, wrinkles and pigmentation such as melasma, leaving smoother, more even skin. Fraxel Restore and Fraxel Dual are non-ablative models using a 1550 nm erbium fiber laser, with the Dual adding a 1927 nm thulium wavelength aimed at superficial pigment.

Laser energy is delivered as microscopic columns, leaving the skin between them intact so healing is faster than with full-surface lasers, and the body remodels the treated zones with new collagen. Published studies, mostly small clinical series, report improvement in these indications, and a large series also catalogued side effects. It is categorised as a professional skin-quality procedure in looksmaxxing discussion.

paras: Clinics perform it as a series of sessions, with skin renewing over days to weeks and several days of recovery after each. It is a medical-device procedure performed by clinicians, and people often pair it with sun protection and skin care.
Reported effects include redness, swelling, peeling, acne flares, herpes outbreaks and, more rarely, scarring or pigment changes.

chain: Smoother texture, less scarring and pigment
angle.text: Fraxel is used over multiple sessions to improve scars, sun damage and melasma, with skin renewing over days to weeks. The laser creates microscopic columns of treated skin, and the body rebuilds collagen as they heal. Small studies report improvement, and Fraxel Dual adds a wavelength aimed at superficial pigment.

lead: Fraxel is a trademarked line of fractional laser systems for skin resurfacing, built on the principle of fractional photothermolysis: laser energy is delivered as an array of microscopic columns, leaving the skin between them untreated so that healing is faster than with full-surface lasers [1]. Fraxel Restore and Fraxel Dual are non-ablative models using a 1550 nm erbium fiber laser, with the Dual adding a 1927 nm thulium wavelength for more superficial pigment targets [1]. A sibling model, Fraxel Repair, uses an ablative carbon-dioxide laser and is the most aggressive of the three [2].

For appearance, the appeal is skin quality: smoother texture, softened acne and surgical scars, fewer fine lines, and more even tone, from a procedure that does not remove the whole outer layer of skin. Fractional laser resurfacing is used in aesthetic medicine for photodamage, wrinkles, acne and surgical scars, and pigmentation such as melasma [3][4][5][6]. Published studies, mostly small clinical series, report improvement in these indications, and a large series also catalogued side effects including acne flares and herpes outbreaks [7][8].

Within looksmaxxing discussion it is categorised as a professional "hardmaxx" skin-quality procedure. Forum users who discuss it tend to describe it as one step in scar or skin-texture projects, sometimes alongside other procedures, and sometimes with attention to the downtime it requires around training and work [9].

paras: Conventional laser resurfacing treats the entire skin surface; ablative versions vaporise the outer layers and carry long recovery. Fractional photothermolysis instead treats a fraction of the skin at once, creating a grid of microscopic thermal zones, each surrounded by untouched tissue that supplies cells for rapid repair [1][8].

Wikipedia distinguishes three Fraxel variants by depth: Fraxel Restore, a non-ablative 1550 nm erbium glass laser described as the gentlest; Fraxel Restore Dual, which pairs it with a 1927 nm thulium fiber laser; and Fraxel Repair, an ablative 10,600 nm carbon-dioxide laser used for wrinkles around the mouth or eyes [2]. According to Grokipedia, the microscopic zones are roughly 100 to 200 micrometres wide, cover a fraction of the treated area per session, and are absorbed by water in tissue [1]. That account is AI-generated and should be read with care.

Fractional photothermolysis was described in 2004 by Dieter Manstein and Rox Anderson at the Wellman Center for Photomedicine, as a way to produce microscopic thermal injury zones with less downtime than ablative lasers [1]. Wikipedia credits Anderson as inventor on the licensed patent and states that Reliant Technologies developed the Fraxel line in 2004 [2].

Per Grokipedia, Reliant launched the first Fraxel system in 2004; Reliant was later acquired in a deal that created Solta Medical, which introduced the Fraxel re:store Dual in 2009, and Solta was acquired by Bausch Health in 2014 [1]. Grokipedia also reports later clearances for acne and surgical scars and a newer Fraxel FTX model [1]; this account is AI-generated and has not been independently checked.

A 2007 study reported use of fractional photothermolysis for atrophic scars [3], and a 2006 Japanese trial examined it for acne scars [6]. A 1,550 nm fractional erbium fiber laser was studied for facial and non-facial photodamage [5], and a 2005 pilot study examined melasma [4]. A comparison in Asian patients tested different fluences and densities for skin rejuvenation [10].

Studies in darker skin types are of particular interest because of pigment-change risk; a review of pigmentary disorders in Asian skin discusses fractional photothermolysis alongside Q-switched lasers and intense pulsed light as options requiring careful selection [11]. These studies are small and short-term, and results for melasma in particular have been described as variable.

A study of 27 Korean patients with Fitzpatrick types IV or V and moderate to severe facial acne scarring evaluated safety and efficacy of the technique [12]. A 2011 trial of 1550 nm nonablative resurfacing examined facial surgical scars [13].

A study of 50 patients with mild to moderate photodamage gave three treatments at 3 to 4 week intervals, with improvement rated by masked evaluators [5]. A randomized trial also examined fractional laser for photoaging of the hands [14].

The 2005 pilot study treated ten women with melasma that had not responded to earlier therapy, at 1 to 2 week intervals [4]. A later study of ten subjects with epidermal melasma examined histologic and ultrastructural changes after treatment [15].

Some clinics combine Fraxel with other treatments. A 2019 study of 45 patients aged 35 to 52 combined five Fraxel sessions with very low G-prime hyaluronic acid and microbotox, and reported that 98 percent of patients had smoother, brighter skin and 68 percent showed fewer skin defects and fine wrinkles, attributed to the laser component [16]. A 2025 split-face randomized trial in 50 patients, mostly women, tested a vitamin C, vitamin E and ferulic acid serum against saline after non-ablative fractional laser and reported lower erythema scores on the serum side [17]. A separate registered study examines a similar post-laser skincare product [18].

Grokipedia describes a typical course of three to five sessions spaced four to six weeks apart, topical anaesthesia, one to three days of redness and swelling resembling sunburn followed by peeling, and visible improvement over three to six months as collagen production builds [1]. Users on lifting forums who plan resurfacing mention the period of thinner, fragile skin and the need to take downtime from training [9].

A retrospective study of 961 fractional treatments documented complications including acne eruptions and herpes simplex outbreaks, and noted that anecdotal reports describe scarring and pigment change [7][8]. Wikipedia repeats these findings and notes that reports of bad scarring and hyperpigmentation come from a patient review site rather than a clinical study [2]. Grokipedia describes redness and swelling for one to three days followed by peeling [1]. Darker skin types carry higher risk of post-inflammatory pigmentation with laser treatments generally [11].

Human studies include case series on atrophic scars [3], acne scars [6][12], photodamage [5] and melasma [4][15], a split-parameter comparison in Asian skin [10], a randomized trial on hand photoaging [14], and a safety review of 961 treatments [7]. Combination work includes the 45-patient laser, filler and microbotox study [16] and a split-face aftercare trial [17].

Registered trials include a 100-person comparison of lasers for scars [19], a trial of a fractional CO2 laser for perioral wrinkles [20] and an ongoing safety and effectiveness study of skin resurfacing [21]. Trials of fractional laser for hair loss were withdrawn or terminated. Most published work consists of small, often industry-linked series without long-term controls.

timeline.event: Fractional photothermolysis described at the Wellman Center; first Fraxel launched and cleared by FDA [1][2].
Retrospective study of 961 treatments reports side-effect rates [7].
